Test learning against chance per participant and stage

Source: R/fba-test-learning.R
test_learning.Rd

For every participant and learning stage, the function pools the scored trials of the selected blocks across contingency types and tests the number of correct responses against a chance performance with a one-sided exact binomial test. Next to the test, it reports the cut-off: the smallest number of correct responses that passes, given the number of answered trials.

Usage

test_learning(
  scores,
  blocks = NULL,
  alpha = 0.1,
  chance = 0.5,
  silence = FALSE
)

Arguments

scores

Per-participant learning scores, from score_learning().

blocks

NULL (default) to test every block of every stage, or a named list of block numbers per stage, e.g. list(stage1 = 6:10, stage2 = 5:8, stage3 = 4:6). Stages absent from the list are tested across all their blocks.

alpha

Numeric(1). One-sided significance level of each test. Defaults to 0.10.

chance

Numeric(1). Probability of a correct response by guessing. Defaults to 0.5, as every trial of the three-stage designs offers two outcomes.

silence

Logical(1). Suppress the message about the assumptions behind the tests. Defaults to FALSE (recommended).

Value

A tibble with one row per participant and stage, and columns:

id, stage

Participant and learning stage.

first_block, last_block, n_blocks

The blocks that entered the test for this participant.

n_responded

Answered trials across blocks.

n_correct

Correct responses among answers.

p_correct

n_correct / n_responded.

k_crit

Smallest n_correct that passes: the least \(k\) with \(P(X \ge k) \le \alpha\) for \(X \sim Binomial(n_{responded}, chance)\).

p_crit

k_crit / n_responded. The proportion correct that passes the null-hypothesis significance test. It should not be confused with a p-value, compare it with p_correct.

p_value

One-sided exact binomial p-value, \(P(X \ge n_{correct})\).

above_chance

n_correct >= k_crit, equivalently p_value <= alpha.

A participant without any answered trial in a stage gets NA in the test columns, including above_chance.

Details

Test assumptions

Under the null hypothesis, a participant's responses carry no information about which outcome is correct, so every answered trial is correct with chance probability, independently of the block. The null distribution of n_correct is therefore exactly \(Binomial(n_{responded}, chance)\) and it does not depend on how accuracy would change across blocks for someone who learns. Learning changes only the distribution under the alternative, i.e., the power of the test, not its size (the rate at which participants without knowledge succeed).

Two consequences follow from Hoeffding (1956), who compares the number of successes in independent trials with unequal success probabilities to the binomial distribution with the same mean:

  • In the three-stage designs every block holds as many trials for one outcome as for the other. A participant who responds with a bias but without knowledge (e.g., always choosing the left option) is correct on half the tested trials on average, with less dispersion than the binomial, and so passes no more often than alpha. Only whole blocks enter the test, which keeps this balance.

  • A participant whose accuracy rises across blocks passes at least as often as one with constant accuracy at the same mean, provided the expected number of correct responses exceeds k_crit by at least one.

Each stage is tested on its own, with no adjustment of the significance test threshold for multiple comparisons across stages. The question asked by the test is whether the participant learned every stage.

Default alpha

At alpha = 0.10 the cut-off on a 48-trial stage is 29 correct (60.4%), similar to the 60% criterion that Le Pelley et al. (2005) applied to both training stages of their two-stage design. On the 80- and 64-trial stages of To our knowledge, no three-stage study tested Stage 3 against chance, so its cut-off cannot be copied from the literature. At the default, a participant who guesses throughout the three-stage replication passes each stage with probability below alpha, and all three with probability below 0.001.

Messages

Every call states the test, the blocks per stage, and how many participants failed the test in each stage, unless silenced (silence = TRUE).

References

Le Pelley, M. E., Oakeshott, S. M., & McLaren, I. P. L. (2005). Blocking and unblocking in human causal learning. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Animal Behavior Processes, 31(1), 56-70. doi:10.1037/0097-7403.31.1.56

Hoeffding, W. (1956). On the distribution of the number of successes in independent trials. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 27(3), 713-721.
